A **WARNING** is raised at a projected 15-minute demand of **1,125 kW**, which is **90% of the 1,250 kW contract capacity**.

**Why this level:**
- The plant bills on 15-minute average demand against its 1,250 kW contract. [unverified citation removed]
- The warning line is set at 90% of the contract (1,125 kW) as an early-lead buffer before the actual limit, so operators can shed load before demand reaches the contract and triggers a penalty. [unverified citation removed]
- Per the dashboard status rules, WARNING is triggered when projected demand ≥ 90% of contract (1,125 kW), or when the forecast probability of exceeding the contract in the next hour is ≥ 20%. [unverified citation removed]

So 1,125 kW is the demand trigger, chosen as a 10% safety margin below the contract to allow time for load shedding before an actual exceedance.

I have the answer from the tariff glossary.

Demand above the contract capacity is billed at a **premium multiplier on the period's contract price**, applied to the excess kW in the interval:

- The excess over contract is billed at **2× the period's contract price** for the portion up to **10% over** the contract capacity.
- Any demand beyond that (above 110% of contract) is billed at **3× the period's contract price**.

For reference, DemoTronics' contract capacity is **1,250 kW** on a regular contract, so the warning line is at 90% (1,125 kW) and the 10% exceedance threshold is at 1,375 kW. [unverified citation removed]

Note that this exceedance charge is separate from the regular monthly **demand charge**, which is a fixed per-kW charge on the contract capacity regardless of actual use. [unverified citation removed]

I found the answer in the forecasting documentation.

The load forecaster (a LightGBM quantile model) predicts the **change from an anchor** rather than the absolute demand level for one key reason:

**Tree models cannot predict values above anything they saw in training.** At DemoTronics the plant rarely exceeded its 1,250 kW contract during the training data, so a model that tried to predict the demand level directly would never output a value above the historical maximum — meaning it would fail to warn about an exceedance. The first version of the model used a level target and missed the exceedances entirely.

By predicting a **change** instead, the model can add a heat-driven or start-up-driven increment on top of the current load, which lets it flag demand that pushes past the contract.

The anchor is:
- **Short horizons (15 min to 3 h):** the last completed interval
- **Day-ahead:** the same time last week

Two refinements keep the prediction bands honest: quantile crossing is fixed by sorting P10 ≤ P50 ≤ P90 per row, and conformal widening scales the band so 80% of the held-out last 14 days fall inside the P10–P90 range.

[source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model]

I now have the full picture. Here's the operator guidance.

## On a hot afternoon when demand may exceed the contract

**1. Watch the forecast status (act early).**
The forecast gives P(exceed) — the probability demand will exceed the 1,250 kW contract in the next hour. This is the key trigger:
- **P(exceed) ≥ 20%** → raises **WARNING**
- **P(exceed) ≥ 50%** → raises **ALARM**

These warnings give time to act before demand actually peaks, and are most useful on hot afternoons when chillers and the cooling tower rise together. [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Forecast-based warnings]

**2. Pre-cool before the peak (SOP-06).**
Move cooling energy earlier: pre-cool the buildings before the peak window so the chilled-water system has margin, and avoid starting new load during the peak. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Purpose]

**3. If WARNING/ALARM is raised, shed load in playbook order (SOP-03).**
Bring projected 15-minute demand back under 1,250 kW before the interval ends, shedding in this order and stopping once under contract:

| Order | Action | Equipment | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pause EV charging | EV-01 | 100% |
| 2 | Delay next burn-in loading | BI-01, BI-02 | 35% |
| 3 | Raise chilled-water setpoint +1 °C | CH-01, CH-02 | 4% |
| 4 | Lower compressed-air pressure 0.5 bar | AC-01, AC-02, AC-03 | 3.5% |

Never shed the server room, running molders mid-cycle, or reflow ovens with boards inside. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 2: shed in playbook order]

**4. During the peak, keep monitoring.**
Check projected demand every interval; if a warning appears, shed in playbook order; raise the chilled-water setpoint +1 °C (≈4% of chiller load) if the pre-cooling margin allows. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 6: during the peak]

**5. Record and restore.**
Log the time, status, projected demand, actions taken, peak reached and probable cause. Once demand is stable and below 1,125 kW, restore shed actions in reverse order (pressure → setpoint → burn-in loading → EV charging), not all at once. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response > Step 5: restore]

**Also:** pause the EV charging bank before hot-afternoon peaks and resume only when projected demand falls back below 1,125 kW. [source: docs/knowledge/equipment/EQ-13_ev_charging.md#EQ-13 EV Charging Bank Manual > Energy-saving notes]

Note: the exact shed shares above are documented assumptions in the playbook, not measured values. [source: docs/dashboard.md#Dashboard > Single-line diagram > Demand]

## 16 June 2025 Start-up Incident

**Peak demand:** The peak 15-minute demand was **1,324.4 kW** at **08:15**, which was 6% above the 1,250 kW contract capacity [data: get_demand]. Two consecutive intervals exceeded the contract — 1,307.1 kW at 08:00 and 1,324.4 kW at 08:15 [data: get_demand].

**What caused it:** A Monday-morning simultaneous start-up. Ten machines — 3 reflow ovens (RF-01/02/03), 3 injection molders (IM-01/02/03/04), the wave solderer (WS-01), the large chiller (CH-02), and air compressor AC-02 — started together within a 3-minute window (07:57–08:27), totaling **805 kW rated** [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-01_monday_startup.md]. Demand had been only ~540 kW at 07:45, then jumped to 1,307 kW at 08:00 as all machines drew power at once [data: get_demand]. The monitoring system flagged this as a high-severity simultaneous-start event and two demand-exceedance alerts [unverified citation removed].

**What a 15-minute stagger would have achieved:** Re-simulating the same morning with machines started 15 minutes apart would have cut the peak from **1,324.4 kW to 1,141.5 kW** (a reduction of 182.9 kW), bringing demand safely below the 1,250 kW contract and avoiding the exceedance penalty of up to **NT$6,652 (US$208)** [data: whatif_staggered_start].

**Context:** SOP-01 (Monday Start-up) is precisely the procedure meant to prevent this — it calls for staggering start-up groups and records the peak demand and any alert raised; the wave solderer is deliberately placed last to avoid adding to the early peak [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-01_monday_startup.md]. The 16 June start-up bypassed that sequencing, which is why the peak spiked.

Yes, a compressed-air leak was detected in September 2025.

**Detection date:** The night-load baseline detector flagged the leak on **2025-09-09** (detected_at), for a rise that began on 2025-09-03. [data: list_detections]

**Size:** The compressor night base load was up to **18.1 kW** above its usual level, i.e. about **+18 kW around the clock**. [data: list_detections]

**Inspection procedure (SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak):**
1. **Trigger** – the night-load baseline detects a rising compressor load; the loss is clearest at night when production demand is low. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Purpose]
2. **Choose the time** – run the walk-down in a quiet period, ideally at night or on a Sunday, so the leak is the largest part of the flow. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 2: choose the time for the walk-down]
3. **Ultrasonic walk-down** – use an ultrasonic detector along main headers and branches, starting where pneumatic use is heaviest (injection molding); check fittings, quick couplers, hoses, filter/regulator units, drain valves and blow-off nozzles, plus the air dryer area and compressor room. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 3: ultrasonic walk-down]
4. **Tag** – tag each leak with a numbered tag, record location/type/estimated size (small/medium/large), and photograph where practical. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 4: tag]
5. **Repair** – isolate and depressurize the section, replace the faulty fitting/hose/valve, re-pressurize and recheck with the detector, then remove the tag and record the closure. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 5: repair]
6. **Verify** – watch the compressor night load for the next several nights and confirm return to the earlier baseline; if it does not return, repeat the walk-down (leaks may be in more than one place). [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-04_compressed_air_leak.md#SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak > Procedure > Step 6: verify]

Note: the detection was rated **medium severity**, with an estimated impact of about **NT$652,462 (US$20,389)/year**. [data: list_detections]

On **5 November 2025**, the power factor of board **MDB-3** was abnormally low — hovering around **0.85** all day (mean 0.849, range 0.845–0.852 during 08:00–17:00) [data: get_meter_series]. This is well below the board's normal value of about **0.96**.

**What happened:** From 2025-11-03 to 2025-11-12 the MDB-3 capacitor bank tripped, taking the board's power factor from 0.96 down to about 0.84 (incident S8) [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Reference case: incident S8]. The low daytime reading on 5 November is the continued effect of that tripped bank.

**What maintenance should check** (per SOP-05):
- The usual cause is a capacitor bank out of service — check for a **tripped breaker or a blown fuse** on the MDB-3 capacitor bank [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Purpose].
- Isolate the bank, replace the failed fuse/contactor/capacitor, and re-energize; if the failure repeats, keep the bank out and call the electrical contractor for a full inspection [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Procedure > Step 3: restore].
- Then verify the 15-minute PF returns toward its normal ~0.96 and confirm the low power factor rule clears [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Procedure > Step 4: verify].
